author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article 

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.




Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party, 

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was 

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.




The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won 

more seats in Congress than any other

 

—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties, 

gave the right a majority in both houses

.




Two days after the vote, 

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he 

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.




“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”





In addition, whoever won in October would be able to 

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

, 

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.




As a result, after the first-round results came in on 

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.




Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one 

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.




Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.




For Gabriel Rochlin, 

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”




From demoralization to esperançar




Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.

“When we got hit with the news that Flávio had more votes, there was a kind of desperation,” said Nayara Ruiz, a social media strategist with 

280,000 followers on Instagram

. “A huge shock, a feeling of fear, and a replay in our heads of 

2018 [when Jair Bolsonaro was elected].” At first, Ruiz recorded a video about that fear. “And while I was editing it, I started to feel really bad. And I said: I’m not going to post this video, this is not the path I need to take.” She came across a news story about how online fandoms dedicated to Brazilian and international musical artists like 

Taylor Swift, BTS and Anitta were putting their networks at the service of Lula’s campaign. “The moment I saw that, I said: ‘That’s it, I have to talk about this, about esperançar.’”




“Esperançar,” was a term used by Brazilian educator Paulo Freire to mean “hope in action,” as opposed to “esperar,” which in Portuguese means both to hope and to wait.




Ruiz then recorded 

a video

 talking about the fandoms and about esperançar, and why it matters for organizing. She explained that esperançar demands three things: seeing a possible future, understanding that there is a path to that future, and feeling that you can do something to make that path a reality. She wanted to show that there was a path to defeat Flávio if people came together.




The video was 

viewed 5 million times, the most of any she had posted, and brought her 40,000 new followers, Ruiz said. It was one of many videos and posts in the days after the first-round vote that spoke to people’s discouragement and helped turn it into a willingness to act.




Social media activism may have been one of the left’s most innovative strategies in this campaign. A WhatsApp channel called Exército do Lula, or Lula’s Army, was created by André Janones, a federal congressman from the state of Minas Gerais. What set it apart was its scale and its structure. It quickly grew from 

50,000

 

to 

more than 10 million followers

 in less than three weeks, in a country where WhatsApp had been the far right’s most effective tool since Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018 campaign.




“We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




The channel’s growth came as the Lula campaign charged that Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, had limited the reach of Lula’s posts and favored Flávio’s. (

Leaked communications from inside Meta

 supported this, and Meta acknowledged “technical problems” with the Lula campaign’s paid promotions, but denied any bias.) For Lula’s Army, the WhatsApp channel had the advantage of delivering messages directly to its followers without an algorithm throttling their reach.




Rather than relying on a few official accounts to broadcast the Lula campaign’s message, it turned millions of ordinary supporters into active participants. It also gamified the organizing for the second round. Because voting is compulsory in Brazil, the goal was less to get out the vote than to reduce abstention and win over undecided voters. Through frequent audio messages, videos and texts, Janones handed out missions to participants, calling on them to share content, boost posts, promote hashtags, invite new members and amplify messages supporting the campaign. Everyone was given a rank and could advance up the ladder by completing these tasks. Janones “promoted” Ruiz from soldier to captain of the Army in a 

lighthearted video

 because of the explainer videos she made about the channel.




She believes one of the initiative’s contributions was fostering a kind of political digital literacy among supporters. Janones taught the channel’s followers how platform algorithms work, so that messages from Lula and critical information about Flávio would rank higher on social media. Until then, the far right had dominated social media, partly because of the high engagement its posts generated. Participants in Lula’s Army came to understand that part of that engagement came precisely from their reacting to far-right content that bothered them.




Previous Coverage

 

How a strong messaging strategy helped defeat Brazil’s Bolsonaro




Janones’ strategic directive to Lula’s supporters was that they should stop interacting with opponents’ posts and concentrate their collective strength on producing and circulating their own content. To that end, participants were instructed to watch videos to the end, and to like, comment on, save and share posts, using the platforms’ different features to expand their reach.




“Maybe Lula wouldn’t have won without this, without the Army, without this feeling that swept over people, without the sense that we weren’t fighting alone,” Ruiz said. “We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




Ruiz credits Janones with turning that collective energy into a coordinated effort. “Janones calls himself a general, but I also see him very much as a conductor who led an orchestra that was disorganized, who tuned the instruments and managed to set the rhythm and organize the whole mobilization that took place and that is now being replicated around the world,” Ruiz said.




Taking to the streets




Social media also played an important role in spreading the word about and organizing the occupation of the streets during the weeks before the runoff. In the three weeks between Oct. 4 and Oct. 25, 

massive peaceful protests

 brought together hundreds of thousands of demonstrators across the country. 

These 

protests featured politicians, renowned Brazilian musicians

 like Chico Buarque, Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil, and grassroots artistic groups. Together, the iconic faces and grassroots artists helped bring in a very broad diversity of people.




“As we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”





University students played a fundamental role in this occupation of the streets. They were the ones who kicked things off on Oct. 5, and throughout the three weeks between the first and second round of voting, they were a major force calling people to the protests, often organizing through their own social media.




The 

first street protest of the runoff campaign took place in Niterói

 in the state of Rio de Janeiro on Oct. 5, organized by students from Fluminense Federal University. Those students set an example, according to Gabriel Shpielman, a mathematics student and activist with the Rebellious Youth Union. “I think if that hadn’t happened on the first day, it would have been totally different,” he said.




Student mobilization quickly spread to other universities, including the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, or PUC-Rio, which also began organizing the day after the first round. Shpielman and a classmate created an Instagram profile and called on students at the university to attend an assembly, from which the 

PUC-Rio Antifascista

 movement was born. Around 200 students packed the auditorium, heard from a representative of the National Union of Students 

a

nd decided to go together to the protest in downtown Rio the following day.




According to Shpielman, this helped “put people in the position of seeing themselves building the comeback.” For him, it was in this experience with their collective strength that fear gave way to organizing: “At first it reflected despair, but as we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”




The call for student protest started by word of mouth, in classrooms and WhatsApp groups, and gained reach through PUC-Rio Antifascista’s Instagram account. The account shared collaborative posts — Instagram posts that appear on several accounts at once — with other accounts, like 

Protesto Estudantil

 (a page run by high school students from Colégio Pedro II), 

the PUC-Rio Graduate Students’ Association, and with public figures such as Dani Balbi, Anielle Franco, Wagner Moura and Chico Buarque.




Students march in a rally for Lula at PUC-Rio on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Tatiana Chain)




Shpielman called the process cyclical: The more visibility PUC-Rio Antifascista gained, the more partnerships it secured, and those partnerships increased its visibility. The page has now reached over 30,000 followers. Even so, for him, social media was at the service of the streets. “What really turned the election around were the streets, the protests,” he said. “Social media reflected that mobilization. It’s so much better to see a protest with a million people than a page with 10 million people.”




Getting voters to the polls




Another point of concern in the first round was the abstention rate, which was the highest since 1998: Over 

21 percent

 of eligible voters, or 33.4 million people, simply didn’t vote. In light of this, much of civil society’s mobilization sought to make sure people went to vote. This took place through 

crowdfunding drives

 to arrange transportation for those living far from their polling places, ride-sharing initiatives, providing information for undecided voters in the streets and vira voto campaigns.




Diego Zuculin is one of the founders of 

Casa Marighella

, a cultural and artistic production company and organization in São Paulo that put all of its work on hold to get out the vote. After the first-round results, “everyone looked at each other and said: ‘Wow, we’re screwed. What are we going to do?’,” Zuculin said. The next morning, the team decided “almost everything could be postponed in the face of the end of democracy.”




The first idea was simple: He would offer his own car to neighbors whose grandparents had no way to get to the polls, and a friend would offer his motorcycle. They soon realized that many people were probably thinking the same thing and decided to create a platform connecting those who could offer rides on election day with those who needed them. That’s how 

Carona Solidária

, or Solidarity Ride, was born.




The team developed the first version of the platform in-house in two or three days. As word spread, partner collectives, artists, tech people and lawyers joined to help with legal issues and with outreach. The platform circulated on Instagram and WhatsApp, and in a second phase, the group reached out to journalists and pages in Brazil’s North region, where there were still few ride offers.




“The heart of vira voto is its humanity. It’s a place for building bonds, for looking people in the eye.”




“We had an idea, we put it to work, then it went to social media and it spread across all of Brazil,” Zuculin said. 

A total of 22,000 rides were offered, in every state and the Federal District, and the real reach was even greater. “Some people told us: ‘I registered two people, but I took two, and on the way back I took three more, and then five more.’ One person posted a video saying they drove 13 people, another 15, and only registered one or two.”




He also says that the reasons users gave when requesting a ride — such as a distant polling place, no nearby buses, advanced age or having to work on election day — could serve as a basis for public policy. In the second round, abstention fell to 

19.22 percent

, the lowest for a runoff since 2006, the result of an effort of which, Zuculin acknowledges, Carona Solidária was only one part.




Complementing these efforts, numerous vira voto campaigns took place across the country, in which people organized in groups to go out on the streets and talk to voters, especially those who were undecided or planning to abstain. Lula himself issued this call 

in a video posted on Oct. 7

: “Come on, everyone, to the streets, let’s talk to people.” 




In Rio de Janeiro, the local WhatsApp group that Gabriel Rochlin belonged to started with fewer than 10 people and ended with 60. Over two and a half weeks, according to the group’s own count, they flipped 181 votes. “Thinking of vira voto as collective action gives you a much greater sense of accomplishment,” he said. The group set up at Largo do Machado square and in front of the Catete Palace because, according to Rochlin, Workers’ Party congressman-elect Marcelo Freixo had indicated that there were many undecided voters there. WhatsApp was used to organize the actions and to make sure volunteers were always together and in safe places, given the risk of violence.

In their conversations, they used QR codes linking to informational materials, such as 

videos from Revelando

, an investigative documentary series launched in September by the Brazilian podcast Calma Urgente in which well-known Brazilian figures voiced criticisms of Flávio. They also 

encouraged people to search Google for information about Flávio

, something that Lula’s Army also urged voters to do. More than the information, however, Rochlin believes that “the heart of vira voto is its humanity. It’s a place for building bonds, for looking people in the eye.”




Oct. 25, the day of the runoff vote, went down in history. Brazilians achieved the unprecedented: They overturned the first-round result, elected Lula and halted the far right’s advance in just three weeks. The internet was flooded with powerful images — streets completely packed with peaceful demonstrations by Lula voters, the elderly voting, people journeying long distances to cast their votes, and entire Indigenous communities traveling to reach their polling places.




Ultimately, the movement to reelect Lula succeeded through a diverse range of civil resistance tactics. Right away, Lula supporters saw that to contain the far right’s advance, it was necessary to occupy the streets, deluge social media and create support structures so that people would vote and could reach the polls. They also saw the importance of mass participation: People from a broad range of social groups — of different ages, genders, social classes and regions of Brazil — acted together. 

In “

Why Civil Resistance Works

,” Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan 

identify mass participation like this as one of the key factors explaining why civil resistance is more likely to succeed than armed struggle.




But one insight runs through all these actions: People need esperançar, the capacity to transform fear into action. Millions organized and, following Paulo Freire’s advice, resisted when it felt hopeless. The far right, which has been advancing in many parts of the world, constantly uses hopelessness as a tool. Brazil’s civil mobilizations shows that esperançar is political, capable of acting as an engine of organization, social action and transformation.

author: Mark Engler
title: Democrats should wield their power to return agency to ordinary people
content:
This article 

Democrats should wield their power to return agency to ordinary people

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Too often, we have seen a fundamental asymmetry at work: When Democrats win power, they might pass a modest minimum wage increase. When Republicans are in power, they do things like decimate public sector unions. In the long term, this is an imbalance that leads to ruin. 




Last week’s “blue tsunami” represented a resounding repudiation of the Trump agenda. While it is common that a sitting administration will lose seats in the midterm elections, swings of the magnitude that we have just witnessed are rare and important. For certain, Trump will still try to use the executive branch to wreak havoc on democracy and provide egregious giveaways for  the billionaire class. However, Democratic control of the Senate and the investigatory power of its majority in the House should provide an important check on his ability to do damage. 




Perhaps more importantly, progressive forces made critical gains at the state level. The Democrats 

won six new “trifectas”

: in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Now, if current leads in Kansas and Alaska hold, “about 75 percent of Americans will live in states with Democratic governors,” and roughly 53 percent will reside in places where Democrats control both chambers of the state legislature as well, 

Newsweek

 

reports

.




Of course, we should not assume that Democrats will use their newfound power effectively if left to their own devices. There are significant blocs of the Democratic Party wherein centrist politicians have made careers of “playing to the middle” and embracing pro-corporate neoliberal politics. Should this tendency prevail, the Democrats will have squandered a historic opportunity, to the detriment of social movements and the broader American public alike.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Forging an alternative path will mean pushing newly empowered legislators to think and act differently. Passing policies that make a real difference in the lives of working people is critical; however, this is only a first step. For movements for social and economic justice to secure long-term wins, they need to be advocating for how they — and their allies in office — can pursue structural reforms. 




A few years ago, after the 2022 midterms, my brother Paul and I wrote an article 

looking at the trifecta power

 that Democrats had gained in multiple states and asking, “Will they actually use it?” More specifically, it asked whether they would use their mandate “to enact changes that increase democratic participation and build progressive power” over the long haul.




When Republicans have gained majorities at the state level “they have used their power to push through reforms that weaken left-leaning constituencies and undermine the Democratic base,” we wrote at the time. “In contrast, when Democrats have been in the majority, they often have failed to reverse these changes or enact meaningful structural reforms — the kind of changes that both improve people’s lives and build power for the grassroots groups that can help them govern on an ongoing basis.” 




Structural reforms can come in many varieties: labor rights, campaign finance issues, measures to encourage and expand voting, redistricting, preemption laws determining whether issues are handled at the state or local level, free speech protections, regulatory modifications that allow for community involvement, and changes to the tort system, to name just a few. More than the specific issue or need addressed by a policy, being attuned to structural reforms means paying attention to how a change gives grassroots forces greater room to maneuver and reach for more in the future.




For social movements, structural reforms are a key mechanism of 

inside-outside politics

, through which grassroots organizations work to elect champions into office who then, in turn, use the power of government to strengthen democratic participation and boost outside campaigns for social justice. Unfortunately, the right often has a better understanding of this process than liberals do.




A dramatic example of how Republicans used statewide governing power to alter the balance of forces was how Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, upon gaining a trifecta in 2010, sought to permanently kneecap unions. Recognizing the importance of organized labor as a foundational part of the Democratic coalition, conservatives made Wisconsin a so-called “right-to-work” state. They also passed the notorious Act 10, which severely restricted the bargaining rights of public sector unions and subjected them to an onerous series of requirements to even continue existing. As a result, these unions lost approximately 70 percent of their members by 2021.




In contrast, when it comes to fighting back, Democrats have a distressing track record of failure and self sabotage. When Iowa Gov. Chet Culver presided over a Democratic trifecta in 2008, he vetoed a bill restoring labor rights, despite having run on a promise to reverse right-to-work. In his fecklessness, he was joined by Colorado Gov. Bill Ritter, who similarly vetoed several pro-union measures, despite having heavily relied on the support of the labor movement to gain office. Both ended up being one-term governors.




In understanding the difference in outcomes, we need only consider what conservative anti-tax leader Grover Norquist 

chillingly wrote

 about the impact of Republican actions in Wisconsin: “Trump’s tweets attract attention,” he remarked. “Act 10 moves forward. Quietly. Inexorably. Changing the political landscape like a glacier.”




Previous Coverage

 

Making our demands both practical and visionary




Democrats commonly talk about reforms that might help people in their everyday lives, like improving public education or incentivizing developers to create more affordable housing, but they don’t focus on shifting power in the long term. “Even in trifecta states, Democrats’ strategy still amounts to playing defense,” Paul and I wrote. “Going on offense would entail learning from the Right’s unashamed boldness. It would mean using Democratic majorities to build social movements and redistribute power and resources in a more durable way — putting a premium on the types of changes sometimes discussed as ‘

policy feedback loops

’ or theorized by socialists as ‘

non-reformist reforms

.’”




Which brings us to today. In the last two years, we have seen a relentless program from Trump not just to advance conservative policy objectives, but to punish social movements and shift the balance of power in favor of reactionaries. Much of this has happened at the federal level, although it has often been backed up by state-level action. The administration has continued the broader Republican strategy of systematically attacking unions, 

ending

 collective bargaining rights for over one million federal employees, and advancing a broad slate of 

anti-worker policies

. 




But while the labor movement is a critical 

pillar of support

 for the left that has been under siege, it is hardly the only one. Trump has systematically targeted social institutions perceived as refuges of progressive values, such as universities and the nonprofit sector. The administration launched an 

assault on large law firms

 that might once have filed lawsuits to help provide some accountability for administration misdeeds. He has likewise aggressively sought to restrict voting rights, encouraged Republicans to pursue new heights of gerrymandering, terrorized the immigrant community, and worked to criminalize dissent.




Each of these moves has something in common. They do not merely aim to enact conservative policies; they seek to permanently consolidate the power of right-wing groups and weaken the ability of any opposing institutions to resist.




In this election, the Republican attempts to entrench themselves failed to overcome the backlash generated by an unpopular war, high gas prices and increased cost of living, Trump’s brazen corruption, and the shocking federal occupation of major cities in the name of immigration enforcement. Movements worked hard to fuel this backlash, but we cannot count on such dramatic surges in public disgust to appear regularly. And we should not underestimate the impact of structurally minded maneuvers, which at times have protected conservatives from successful democratic challenge for decades.




The need for progressive movements and their elected allies to pursue structural reforms is not about tit-for-tat retaliation. There is a fundamental difference between enacting changes designed to reinforce privilege, profit, minority rule and the power of the wealthy, and those designed to expand voting rights, bolster democratic participation, and increase the ability for ordinary people to have a voice in their workplaces and in the public sphere alike. The goal of structural reforms by progressives is not to consolidate the power of a tyrant like Trump, but to increase power that is wielded democratically. Indeed, the danger is that centrist Democrats — themselves beholden to wealthy donors and often susceptible to 

threats

 of capital flight — prove unwilling to challenge fundamentally anti-democratic forces when given the opportunity.
















Support Us

Donate













There have been some reasons for hope — and some examples of what the pursuit of structural changes can look like. Responding to a concerted campaign by organized labor, Michigan Democrats did, in fact, 

reverse

 their state’s “right-to-work” law in 2023, making Michigan the first to ever do so. The victories of progressives in Minnesota, who used inside-outside strategies to pass a variety of important gains, including expanded organizing and voting rights, is also a model that has become 

increasingly heralded

 in recent years. 




In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has 

created

 an Office of Mass Engagement, meant to encourage people to actively involve themselves in city politics outside of elections, and an 

Office of Worker Power

, designed to help workers exercise their rights to organize. These are important examples of how government can seek to strengthen grassroots movements, even as it delivers on issues of affordability. 




Overall, the yardstick by which we measure Democratic progress should not just be whether the policies they pass provide immediate benefits, but how these initiatives serve to reduce corporate power and return political agency to ordinary people. 




The damage that Trump has wrought will not be easily reversed. But if progressive movements are to revitalize democracy and reverse trends toward oligarchic rule, we must think structurally and push for the kind of reforms that build power that can last for more than one wave.

author: Stephen Lerner
title: Trump and technofascism took a hit — now we must act
content:
This article 

Trump and technofascism took a hit — now we must act

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The midterm election was a repudiation of Trump and of his Silicon Valley billionaire enablers. This has created a huge opening that we should celebrate — yet we should be clear-headed about the challenges ahead. Victory over Trumpism and Silicon Valley technofascism is by no means assured. Trump’s 

appointment of Stephen Miller, a white nationalist

, to chief of staff is a flashing warning sign. 




Trump and Miller have massive power to use the Justice Department, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, and other tools of the federal government to target Trump’s opponents. And the Silicon Valley billionaires will use their extraordinary wealth and power to try to crush attempts to stop the build-out of massive data centers, which they desperately need to power their AI expansion. There are growing fears that AI investments have created a stock market bubble that is leaking and ready to burst. The $2.5 trillion sell-off of AI and tech stock on Nov. 5 is a terrifying illustration of how 

AI speculation may crash the whole economy

. So while we should breathe in the hope the electoral results have delivered to us, we must also redouble our resolve and prepare for the battles ahead.




Over the past two years, many of us felt overwhelmed, strangled and suffocated by unrelenting attacks that came from every direction, from ICE kidnapping our neighbors, to the U.S. bombing and warring on other countries, to absurd conspiracy theories and racist ranting by Donald Trump, Elon Musk and their ilk. As we can now see, the increasingly vicious nature of their words and actions was also a sign of their weakness and growing desperation. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










But weakness and desperation should not be confused with surrender. As our history reminds us, the forces of entrenched power and wealth are nothing if not resilient. They will use every tool at their disposal to deflect or dilute reform, divide their opponents, and prepare countermoves that will roll back our gains. The Reconstruction of the post-Civil War years gave birth to the reactionary “Redeemers,” who succeeded in undoing efforts to advance racial equality. The forward thrust of the New Deal was blunted by the Red Scare. The civil rights gains of the 1960s were challenged by the Southern Strategy and the Reagan Revolution.   




So we should prepare ourselves for the reality that the forces that we have been fighting will not simply throw in the towel. We should not assume that the lawless ways of the Trump presidency will suddenly cease or that its billionaire backers will retreat to the comfort of their gated communities and private jets and cease their efforts to commandeer our future. Far from it. We must expect that they will use every bit of the considerable power they still hold to thwart real change.  




Silicon Valley AI billionaires have made clear that they aren’t content with just becoming billionaires and trillionaires. Their goal is far more expansive and scary. They want to eliminate democracy altogether and replace it with a CEO autocracy. Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel is worth $37 billion and publicly says, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” 




Defunding AI




The election has shown that the popular mood is behind us. We have a unique window to thwart the Silicon Valley billionaires and to build and exercise power. None of us has a road map of how to do this, but there are some promising paths we can take. A central task is figuring out how we stop funding, bankrolling and purchasing from the technofascist billionaires. We need to stop financing our own destruction. 




There are a series of exciting campaigns already happening 

that are trying to do exactly that, and each one offers opportunities for people to be involved individually and organizationally. These campaigns offer, if successful, a vehicle to organize and activate hundreds of thousands of new activists directly in the fight for democracy and against the Silicon Valley AI overlords. 




Previous Coverage

 

10 reasons to resist AI




The $6 trillion of public employee pension fund assets and $900 billion in university endowments are currently a key 

source of capital

 for Musk and other oligarchs. We need to cut off, or at least limit, the massive flow of capital to the AI oligarchs and drivers of data center construction. It is a form of assisted suicide for union pension funds and public employee pension funds to invest in the very corporations whose goal is to destroy unions and public sector jobs and services. 




Unions and union members have a central role to play in protecting their pensions from AI investments that are both risky and self-defeating. They should call for this money to be invested in things like affordable housing and green retrofitting programs that create good union jobs, address pressing issues like climate change and the housing crisis, and support local economic development. Members can start speaking up en masse at public pension board meetings. Local unions can pass resolutions like the Chicago Teachers Union did in October 2025, with a 

“Resolution For A Pension Fund that Provides A Dignified Retirement While Promoting a More Just Society.”

   




Students and higher education workers have an opportunity to challenge heavy investment by many university endowments in AI. The University of Michigan was one of the first investors in OpenAI. The University of North Carolina 

holds significant shares in SpaceX

 SuperIntelligence after the merger of SpaceX with xAI in February. The UNC fund made its initial SpaceX investment through Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel’s Silicon Valley “Founders Fund,” which heavily funds AI start-ups. Duke University also has $70 million in assets tied to the Founders Fund.




The work challenging these investments has already started with the Action Center on Race and the Economy’s 

Stop Funding Billionaires

 campaign, which is organizing members of unions and community groups to oppose continued investments in AI and bad corporate actors. Stop Funding Billionaires is working with Americans For Financial Reform, the American Association of University Professors, California Common Good, the People’s Lobby and others to halt Anthropic’s upcoming trillion dollar initial public offering. 




The 

#BlockTheIPO campaign

 is calling on banks, institutional investors and stewards of public funds to boycott the Anthropic IPO, to pause all investment in AI and data centers, and to pledge not to bail out AI companies with public taxpayer and retirement funds until the financial and safety risks of AI are addressed. The campaign has combined research exposing the dangers of AI investment with direct action and protests targeting both Anthropic’s offices and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, whose bank is part of a syndicate of banks underwriting the IPO.  




Protestors gathered outside of OpenAI’s office in New York City to demand a pause on AI and data center development. (Gina Randazzo)




Labor has another critical role to play in this by adopting the approach of 

Bargaining for the Common Good, or BCG

. BCG builds power by bringing unions and their community allies together around shared demands that benefit both workers and communities. When it comes to corporate accountability, BCG can look like organizing and bargaining 

campaigns that target the financial powers

 — Wall Street, private equity, hedge funds — whose influence determines the behavior of corporate CEOs and government officials alike. Such campaigns provide a model that can facilitate the alignment of labor unions and popular movements against the rampant spread of data centers, and in 

defense of democracy

.




This isn’t an exhaustive summary, but it gives a feel for what is developing and what roles we can play. We are educating and organizing an army of union members, students and higher education workers to demand no more investments from pensions and university endowments in AI tech corporations.




Democracy defense




Even as we push back on data centers, we must also continue to challenge corporations whose actions have been eroding our democracy. Cities and states should stop using our tax dollars to subsidize, buy from or give tax breaks to companies that have won Trump administration contracts through corrupt “pay to play” procurement practices. Municipalities should also stop enriching corporations carrying out Trump’s authoritarian agenda. 

Not with Our Money

 is working with elected leaders and allies around the country to halt purchasing from companies like Palantir that are powering the surveillance state, ICE’s deportations and detention centers. 




Another example of this work is the global 

Purge Palantir

 campaign, which is fighting the spread of the surveillance state and the model of algorithmic governance. It’s calling public and private sector employers to stop using Palantir products and politicians to refuse political contributions from Palantir. Similarly, 

Tesla Takedown

 has focused on Elon Musk and Tesla and has conducted nonviolent protests at dealerships around the country to protest Musk’s many nefarious activities, beginning with his stint dismantling the government through DOGE.




Campuses should also organize to expose university investments in private equity companies that have teamed with Trump to threaten the future of higher education. The University of Michigan and Washington University are two of many examples of endowments that have invested in the private equity company Apollo, despite CEO Marc Rowan’s role as a key architect and promoter of the Trump administration’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education” — an attempt to enforce ideological conformity, censorship and political oversight on universities, including an unconstitutional loyalty oath. 




The 

All Eyes on Yass

 campaign is organizing to make it unacceptable for politicians who want labor and community support to take contributions from billionaires like Jeff Yass who are spending millions supporting school vouchers and undermining public education. Like the 

Purge Palantir

 campaign, the All Eyes on Yass campaign is telling politicians they have to pick which side they are on.




The path to the future we want and need is certainly more open today than it was only a week ago. But we have a long and treacherous road ahead and significant obstacles to overcome.  




Building our immune response to fascism 




As I think about the challenge that confronts us, I think of a lesson I have had to learn the hard way. You see, I am allergic to bees. I have been stung by a yellow jacket, and I know that terrifying feeling of my throat swelling, of feeling the air being cut off, and literally fearing that I could go into shock and die within minutes. It’s the same suffocating feeling many of us in occupied Washington D.C. are experiencing as Flock cameras, ICE, the National Guard, police checkpoints and the surveillance state increasingly impact every part of our lives.




I’ve learned that being deathly allergic to bees means that you can either hide inside, out of fear of being stung, or you can study and learn about bees to limit the possibility of being killed by them. I have made it my business to deeply understand bees, and specifically, the yellow jacket, the only bee that has ever stung me. I’ve learned yellow jackets are most dangerous when they feel their nests are being encroached upon, and that this danger surges in the fall, when the weather is getting colder and they know they will soon die off for the season. They strike out and sting you for no apparent reason when they feel their time is coming to an end. 




I see waning Trumpism as analogous to yellow jackets in autumn. Like yellow jackets facing encroaching winter, those whose support made Trumpism possible know the demographics of the country are changing, that whites won’t always remain in the majority. They fear that we might be developing an immunity to their politics of division and hate. They also know how much their wealth and power depends on the bailouts, theft, fraud and massive financial manipulations that their control of the political system has allowed them. They know that their dominant role in this country and the world can come to an end if they can’t hold onto power now. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













If we are wise enough to grasp their psychology, if we are strategic, if we organize, if we are prepared, if we are inspired and moved by knowing our season is coming, we can do more than just survive this change of seasons. 




For most of my life I’ve carried an Epipen to inject myself if I got stung. A combination of careful avoidance and life-saving injections have kept me alive despite multiple stings. But after learning to accommodate and survive bees, I’ve realized that surviving is insufficient; fear isn’t the way I want to live. So I have started a multi-year course of bee venom injections that over time will make me immune to bee stings. Soon, getting stung by a bee may be a painful annoyance, but it won’t threaten my life.




Similarly, we can start to inoculate ourselves against fascism. That means preparing ourselves to engage in mass noncompliance and nonviolent civil disobedience directed not only at the lawless administration that still holds power, but at the corporations that are supporting and profiting from Trumpism. Each time we engage in non-compliance — standing up to defend our immigrant neighbors from ICE — we start to build our immunity to fear. When we sit-in and engage in nonviolent civil disobedience at a corporate office or an airport, we build the systemic response that can ward off the stings they will no doubt seek to deliver in the weeks and months ahead. I know from my own experience with yellow jackets that they will reemerge in spring if we don’t destroy their nests.







This article 

Trump and technofascism took a hit — now we must act

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

title: The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities
content:
This article 

The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Voters in the midterm elections dealt a decisive blow to Trump’s war agenda and have created new possibilities for challenging militarism and ending the debacle in Iran. The blue tsunami that swept across the country was driven by 

many issues

, including tariffs, corruption and higher prices, but voter discontent was rooted in opposition to the war against Iran and the high fuel costs and inflation that resulted. 




The election outcome presents an opportunity for activists to intensify pressures to end the war, reverse excessive arms spending, restore necessary funding for vital social and environmental priorities, and protect democracy. We need to elect a government that will build the foundations for a forward-looking, progressive foreign policy by expanding essential diplomatic capabilities and restoring U.S. support for global cooperation.




The current electoral realignment can be compared to the dramatic political transformation that occurred in the 2006 midterm elections. That year, the Iraq war was the 

decisive issue

 in helping Democrats pick up 31 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and six in the Senate. Then as now, affordability and immigration were important issues, but the dominant concern was war in the Middle East. As analysts argued at the time, Iraq was the “

Archimedean lever

” that shifted voters toward Democrats. 




But when the new Congress assembled in 2007, Democratic Party leaders equivocated. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid proposed a legislative agenda for the new Congress that ignored Iraq. 




Embed from Getty Images




As Tom Hayden wrote in  “Ending the War in Iraq”, antiwar activists were furious. Constituents bombarded Democratic leaders with demands to prioritize withdrawal from Iraq. Protesters gathered outside Pelosi’s San Francisco home. An estimated 100,000 people marched in an antiwar rally in Washington, D.C. 




Democratic leaders quickly got the message and agreed on a legislative strategy to establish a timetable for withdrawal, which Congress subsequently adopted. 




We may need to exert similar pressures now to ensure that the new Congress fulfills its political mandate to end the Iran war and takes action to reverse other elements of Trump’s dangerous foreign policies. 




The threats to peace have grown significantly in recent years, and they are enormous and multifaceted. An unending, illegal war in Iran and related carnage throughout the Middle East; the arming of repressive regimes, up to and including enabling genocide in Gaza and occupation and ethnic cleansing in Lebanon; the skyrocketing of military-related spending (proposed at more than 

$1.5 trillion

 this year) and an accelerating nuclear arms race. All of this is occurring while the Pentagon is 

moving

 rapidly towards the deployment of AI-driven weapons systems that can operate without human pilots or human control.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










The threat or use of force has taken precedence over diplomacy, economic development and peacebuilding programs. The White House has rebuked democratic allies in Canada and Europe while coddling authoritarian regimes in Russia and Saudi Arabia. 




The human, economic and environmental consequences of these militarist policies have been disastrous — 

trillions

 of dollars wasted, 

hundreds of thousands

 of lives lost and 

tens of millions

 of people driven from their homes.      




The pursuit of peace abroad depends on the defense of democracy at home. Legislators must protect democracy by removing obstacles to the exercise of basic rights, including the right to vote, the right of assembly, freedom of speech and an end to discrimination based on race, gender, religion and sexual preference. We need to create an America where every person is cherished, and every person is treated with the dignity they deserve — and then we need to extend that ethos to the rest of the world.




For cooperation, not confrontation




On the foreign policy front, we must demand congressional and executive action on the following major goals:




1. End the Iran war

: Prohibit the use of funds for military hostilities over, in, or off the shores of Iran. Work through the United Nations to reach a comprehensive diplomatic agreement to open the Strait of Hormuz and contain Iran’s nuclear program. Close vulnerable American military bases in the region.  




2. Halt and reverse the arms race

: Enact major reductions in the bloated Pentagon budget, roll back spending on nuclear weapons systems and rein in the rush towards automated warfare based on artificial intelligence. Block funding for renewed nuclear testing and the production and deployment of additional nuclear warheads.




3. Stop arming genocide and repression

: Cut military aid and arms transfers to Israel that violate U.S. human rights law and enable genocidal policies in Gaza, and accelerate dispossession and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and aggression in Lebanon. Stop providing arms and aid to repressive and undemocratic regimes in the region. Terminate the Saudi nuclear deal.




4. Roll back the war at home

: End militarized immigration enforcement, the unlawful detention of immigrants and ICE repression — including murder — of peaceful protesters. ICE should be eliminated as part of a thorough revamping of immigration policy.




Together these points form a peace agenda that lays the foundations for a progressive foreign policy that rebuilds critical diplomatic capacities and U.S. support for multilateralism.




Congress already started to take action on some of these priorities, even under Republican majorities. And the Democrats in Congress have started to take stronger stands against endless war and excess military spending in a way that has not happened in decades. In June of this year, the Senate joined the House of Representatives in 

adopting House Concurrent Resolution 86 

under the War Powers Act, directing the President to end military hostilities in Iran, although the White House ignored the order. 




In July Senate Democrats 

refused to authorize

 the bloated $1.15 trillion request for funding of routine Pentagon operations over concerns about the Iran war. Congress needs to follow through in the lame duck session to oppose any increases in the Pentagon’s topline budget. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Also in July, almost half of the Democratic members of the House voted to eliminate U.S. aid for Israel as part of 

groundswell of opposition

 to Israeli policy in Gaza. Congress must follow through with actions to end U.S. complicity with war crimes. Prospects for success on these and related legislative measures in the new Congress will increase with the arrival of dozens of new representatives and senators elected on a mandate against endless war. But success is not assured.




A new Congress as a new beginning




While the realignment of Congress in the midterm election is a victory for sanity and peace, it is only the beginning of the struggle that lies ahead. To become law, the peace agenda needs the backing of a strong, growing movement of coordinated national and grassroots public action. This will require dialogue and relationship-building across the various movements fighting for justice and peace, a process that is already underway in many places.  




We must demand that the leaders of the new Congress prioritize the proposed peace agenda, as part of a pivot toward developing and reinvesting in an alternative foreign policy for peace. If the newly elected members waffle or refuse, we should protest in Washington, D.C. and assemble at their local offices to demand that they act. 




We will need to undertake coordinated and systematic efforts to brief new members of Congress on the key issues and the legislative options for ending the war in Iran, reversing America’s militarized priorities and preventing oppression and violence in the Middle East. 




Plans are needed in the coming weeks and months to convene community meetings and teach-ins on the proposed peace policy agenda — both at the national level and in dozens of key states and districts. It is essential that members of Congress hear the demand for change not only from lobbyists in Washington, D.C.  but from voters in their home districts.




Embed from Getty Images




We need to be clear that creating a new foreign policy means more than an end to Trumpian policies, as unconscionable as they are and have been. America’s penchant for war without public or congressional consent has persisted under presidents of both parties, as has unstinting support for Israel’s brutal conduct in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and Iran, as well as the repression and political machinations of oil rich states like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. 




To craft a new foreign policy, we need more than the absence of Trump.  We need the presence of an alert, mobilized citizenry committed to radically changing America’s approach to the world. Our mission is to turn our country toward diplomacy and international cooperation rather than war, and to hold officeholders of both parties to that standard.




We need a foreign policy of, by, and for the people — all of us, not just a narrow, self-interested, corrupt elite. Foreign policy should serve the aspirations of everyone for peace, sustenance and basic human rights, regardless of race, religion, place of origin, gender or sexuality. Not just changing America but also joining hands with movements and peoples around the world in struggles for peace and democracy against war and repression.




This article 

The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: Daniel Hunter
title: Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
content:
This article 

Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: a massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins. 




This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred 

three times since World War II

 (1946, 1994 and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding: 

the first Native American governor and senator

, 

five Black governors

, the first 

majority of Democratic governors in 16 years

, and critical downballot wins like the first Democrat to win as 

Texan oil regulator since 1990

 and the 

first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama

.




Authoritarians do not do well when trapped — and with a famously norm-busting president, anything is possible. But, critically, election deniers like 

Darline Graham

 and 

Greg Abbott

 are conceding their races. Donald Trump is already saying he’s 

“absolutely willing”

 to accept the results and 

told CBS

, “Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”




So what do we do now?




1. It’s OK to exhale




These midterms have left me, like many, with abundant free-floating anxieties. The 

“what if” scenarios

 have been abundant — and while some of the most extreme versions did not happen, the federal government was weaponized against the election system like never before.




Because the times have been so rough, it can be hard to exhale and accept a win, especially since elections are not material changes — they are promissory notes that the future may be different. Until Jan. 3, we live under the same dangerous authoritarian government, even if the atmosphere has changed.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Before I advocate for you to breathe, let’s affirm all the many hard reasons to not exhale. The wins were not universal, as some big losses cut deep. There’s a reality that all of this is ephemeral if Democrats cannot govern a policy of change — if we only manage an economic status quo it will disillusion and likely result in yet another whiplash election in the other direction. And it’s hard to breathe in a dizzying moment.




Further, the attacks on elections were treasonous. I won’t list the complete litany of federal assaults — but we have a Department of Justice captured by authoritarian forces using its power nakedly for partisan goals. The far right openly prepared 

sham legal theories

 to refuse certification of Democratic representatives. While we did not get systematic federal law enforcement terror at polls, we saw National Guard throughout 

Washington, D.C.

 We still have too many election officials committed to the Big Lie. And ongoing structural impediments to a fair election are consequential: In Mississippi, the Senate margin remains tiny while any win may be marred by 

equipment trouble, poll changes,

 and 

voters unexpectedly removed by data purges from the voting rolls

.  




Notably, the election maps themselves have been gerrymandered by racists to ensure power — though their greed rebounded 

multiple losses

 in these redistricted seats. (Groups like Black Voters Matter deserve a huge shout-out for fighting in the South and in races Democrats had abandoned.)




Despite all that, we managed a pro-democracy win that was too big to rig. The country delivered a shellacking to MAGA politics — an encouraging sign for all of us who are hoping for a better future. Ultimately, the election proceeded with voters refusing to be intimidated.




Buddhists remind me we can take a breath anytime. But this moment seems as good a moment as any, especially when we remind ourselves exhaling isn’t signaling that things are over. Exhales are how our body gets in tune with this moment and releases the latest tension. Bracing doesn’t make us wiser, just tenser.




So really, take five breaths right now. As you breathe, read in a poem by 

Jarod Anderson

: “

You can be still while the world is whirling. / You can be silent while your heart is thundering. / You can be alone while your memory is teeming. / You can live forever in the span of a moment. / You can grow kindness in the soil of hatred. / You can decide purpose. You can decide victory.”




2. Celebrate our unsung heroes




As we breathe in — exhale and inhale — it’s worthwhile to remember the overwhelming number of people standing up to authoritarianism right now.




Previous Coverage

 

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?




Media have focused on tariffs, affordability and the Iran war as the defining issues of the midterms. But, as usual, they’ve skipped over the resistance that has taken root in this country. People lost their livelihoods exposing this regime’s corruption and 

risked their lives resisting ICE

.




We got to this moment thanks to many unsung people.




Here we could begin listing thousands upon thousands of names. The list would include top election officials in all 50 states who refused to be cowed by the DOJ’s threats to arrest them for doing their jobs. (Some of them are quite hilarious, like 

Oregon’s Secretary of State Tobias Read

, who mocked the DOJ hacks who misspelled his name: “my name is spelled R-E-A-D, as in ‘read the Constitution.’”) But those names extend deep through the electoral ecosystem, with many officials running extreme training scenarios steeling themselves against federal overreach, like 

Boulder’s County Clerk and Recorder Molly Fitzpatrick

, and others coming up with creative solutions, like Georgia’s 

Irwin County Election Supervisor Ethan Compton

 who added “panic buttons” for poll workers to get immediate back-up support.




Recognizing how election officials remain under attack, Protect Our Election 

set up

 a way to thank them online, and the National Conference on Citizenship created 

Election Hero Day

 as a “national celebration recognizing the tremendous contributions” of election officials.




But, of course, credit extends beyond officials. It goes to people like 

Keith Odom

, a 62-year-old forklift driver, who joined 

over 5,000

 at the “All Roads Lead to the South” rally in May, pushing back against the Supreme Court’s 

Callais

 decision undoing civil rights legislation. Credit is due to organizers like 

Chanae Jackson of Florida for All

 and 

Bill Hogseth

 of Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin, and 

Cassandra Welchlin

 of Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable who collectively trained thousands of election defenders.




All that worked mattered greatly to avoid the worst scenarios. 




When the FBI raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative — a get-out-the-vote community group in Ohio working primarily with people of color — it could have broken. Instead its director, Prentiss Haney, struck a defiant public stance, naming the raid for what it was: “a political act to try and intimidate people from voting.” The Ohio Organizing Collaborative kept going — and were backed by allies across the nation under the banner of “

Hands Off Ohio

.”




Despite all the threats, voters voted. And that’s thanks to Tobias, Ethan, Molly, Keith, Chanae, Bill, Cassandra, Prentiss, and the tens of thousands who fought to keep the election more fair 

despite

 the authoritarian attempts to subvert them.




Civil resistance researcher Hardy Merriman developed a helpful 

framework

 for understanding the full election cycle in authoritarian times. It’s four steps: Fight, Win, Prove, Enforce. Fight for every legal voter to vote. Win pro-democracy electoral victories. Prove what actually happened and expose manipulation. And finally: Enforce the will of the voters — and stop any attempt to overturn it. 




We don’t get to where we are right now without successfully moving through these early phases — Fight and Win. Take a moment to consider how you’ll appreciate those unheralded heroes — because you can be guaranteed the punditry class largely won’t do them justice.




3. We are entering Prove phase: count every valid vote




The election was decisive, but it’s not over. The current phase of battle includes wrangling over ballot counts — and making sure those counts are understood as significant 

despite

 all the shenanigans.




Anyone in or near a closely contested race can help in this phase by volunteering to cure ballots — the process of helping fix ballots with minor imperfections like a missing signature. Rules vary widely, so contact a local election or campaign office or find efforts at 

We Are Ground Control

.




As of writing, Mississippi is one of the hottest of these races, with Scott Colom on track to win narrowly if a clean election process unfolds, a challenge given the state’s messy, rickety election verification process. The Colom campaign 

feels confident

 that they will win.




Our job remains to be grounded in facts. Turn to trusted, verified reporting, like 

Votebeat

 or 

Brennan Center for Justice

. 

Pause

 before sharing any election information and try to verify its authenticity. And we must remind ourselves that this win was not inevitable, it was “despite” — despite DOJ lawsuits, despite ICE threats, despite gerrymandering, despite consistent attacks on voters, and despite the many ways the federal government tried to keep voters from voting.




While Trump, Vance and MAGA will make up lies, what happens next will depend in part on what their potential 

accomplices

 will do. Some groups like May Day Strong are wisely 

pressuring corporate targets now

, knowing that corporate accomplices make disenfranchisement much easier. They’ve notched some important wins: For example, the entire city of 

Culver City, California

 approved the 

Business for Democracy Pledge

, pledging public business opposition to any post-election shenanigans.




Which reminds us that proving the results doesn’t just happen in courtrooms and elections — it happens in the streets, too.




4. Don’t be scared of taking to the streets




A key lesson here comes from the 2000 presidential contest between George W. Bush and Al Gore. Folks who are old enough remember that it came down to Florida, which was decided by a margin of a few hundred votes out of the six million that were cast. As the recount began, paid Republican operatives screamed and pounded on doors of the Miami-Dade counting office, intimidating staffers and causing a halt to the recount. A history-changing moment unfolded: Democratic operatives told activists to 

not

 go into the streets and protest — 

trust the courts

, they said. The courts sided with Bush, cleared the way to never count the ballots, and the legal coup was cemented. (Three members of 

today’s Supreme Court

 were part of that Republican effort to halt the recount.)




The No Kings movement just proved the value of going to the streets. They experimented with gathering folks for Vote Early Day, to help surge turnout. Indications are this was very critical for the win. A TargetSmart 

analysis

 compared places with and without the No Kings Early Day mobilizations. The results were remarkable: 

a 19 percent increase in turnout for early voting where they had activations

.




So coupling street heat with elections boosted energy and turnout.




Previous Coverage

 

How Serbian students toppled an authoritarian




The pattern affirms what we learned from Serbia and Brazil — in both countries, an unprecedented number of people voted and overcame huge challenges with a drumbeat of protests leading up to the elections. Serbia experienced a record 

70 percent turnout

 and Brazil’s Lula won the 

largest number of votes in Brazilian history

.




A recent 

detailed review

 concludes that anti-ICE/pro-immigrant actions have reached historic levels, even in Trump-won counties. They cite research linking bases of support activated by protests and how they translate into previous midterm outcomes. The authors ask the question: “

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?

” It appears they did.




So while our election infrastructure appears to be holding, our readiness to take to the streets only strengthens our hand. Local Indivisible and 50501 chapters have plans to hold upbeat “Count every vote” rallies (you can 

find ones in your area on Mobilize

). This is wise because it creates a narrative counterweight — especially as MAGA is expected to fill the narrative field with garbage.




Famously, in 2024, Philadelphia responded to Trump’s outrageous threats against the people counting the vote by holding an upbeat dance party outside of the Philadelphia Convention Center — a visible demonstration of countering ugly fear and threats with joy and life.




5. Get ready if we need to Enforce




Trump and Vance have developed a narrative about fraud that they could use to discredit selective election results. We know the DOJ is captured completely by Trump and subject to his whims.




We know Trump is too impulsive not to do something. Reading exactly what he’ll do and where is an exercise in reading tea leaves, but it appears more likely he’s following the path of victimhood, attacking Republicans for their lack of loyalty. Alongside telling the 

New York Times

 that he “look[s] forward to working with” Democrats, Trump has 

posted furiously on TruthSocial

 attacking Greg Abbott for losing because he was a Republican In Name Only, or RINO, writing “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses” or asserting that the Republican Party as a whole would have won if 

he

 was on the ballot.




Alaska remains another state to watch, given MAGA’s claims that Alaska was stolen. For now the courts have rejected the DOJ’s Alaska gambit to force the state to refuse certification if the Republican candidate for Senate loses. And the drumbeat to stop Alaska’s certification has been dulled underneath the electoral avalanche that has descended on the Republican party.




Losing appears to be 

growing Republican in-fighting

. That’s understandable, since Trump is clearly no longer the mighty savior he once appeared to them to be. They, too, need to adjust to the new reality of the end of Trump 2.0 and discover what life under lame-duck Trump is like.




Part of the Enforce phase also means getting the message of the elections right. The most dominant message needs to be: the country looked at fascism and fully rejected it. This door must remain closed — and now we turn our attention to debating how we solve people’s pocketbook issues such that we don’t have a return to fascist populism.




Here are three actions to stay prepared:







Each person in a state with yet-to-be-called races or candidates who have not conceded should find if there are local ways to help with ballot curing and tracking their own state’s 

certification dates

. If you’re not in one of those states, get ready to act in solidarity with other states.




Circle Jan. 3 as a key date to anchor our planning — that’s when Congress is seated and our “end date” of the election cycle.




Get your list of people that you would want to go into the streets with. There likely are local groups you can connect with. 







So if you haven’t already: Write down the names of three or four people you would be willing to go into the streets with if something happens. Talk now about how you will contact one another, how you will make decisions, and what kinds of actions you are prepared to take. Agree on basic commitments: stay nonviolent, check information before acting on it, look after one another, and do not let a rumor become the plan.




To get plugged into national response, 

No Kings has set-up an election pledge

 to join mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed. Mass calls are already prepped for nationwide updates and mobilizations: Nov. 4 a 

No Kings Mass Call

 and Nov. 5 a 

Working Families Party Mass Call

. If you’re looking for more guidance on forming election-protection groups, 

Hold the Line

 and 

Strike Ready

 offer trainings and resources.




6. And then there’s the Sustain phase




Activist Nadine Bloch has helpfully added a fifth phase to Hardy’s model: Since the elections are not an endpoint, we must Sustain — 

which is about sustaining the energy and movement for the long-haul pressure campaigns that come after. We still have a whole body of work in front of us.




One tempting mistake is to waste the bulk of our ammunition against each other. We are not out of the authoritarian woods and the big tent attitude that got us here is still required, even as tensions are going to fray over strategy and direction. 




Still, some reckonings are overdue. In Florida, mainstream Democrats were shocked by Angie Nixon’s primary win and 

canceled their planned unity rally

. Her loss in the general election stings, especially because her organizing juggernaut defied centrist expectations and lifted turnout and downballot wins across the state. Running progressives did not, as some folks worry, result in devastating losses — quite the opposite.




Still it’s unhelpful for anyone to get cocky and claim the American public has embraced their entire platform. This was less a blue wave and more a red repudiation. 




This period of lame-duck Trump presidency remains precarious as progressives, centrists, populists, and anyone at all still have the chance to prove they have ideas that help people’s pocketbooks. Regular folks still want practical problem-solving, but know the system needs more than tweaks to get there.




With Democrats locked out of the executive branch, some policies remain out of reach. We have to communicate that often — so people do not lose sight of the need for a 2028 win and get needlessly discouraged that this moment does not result in faster change.




That means constantly telling a compelling story about the structural problems we face so that the solutions become more evident, while also showing that government can work. Think of Mamdani’s constant videos about the big challenges we face, paired with solving everyday problems like 

fixing potholes

. We got into this authoritarian mess because of much bigger issues than Trump. The social isolation. The drive of capitalism to pull wealth from the Earth and our own pockets. The way politics drives wedges between communities. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













All these problems require big structural fixes and strengthening local civic relationships. There is work everywhere and, as Nadine reminds us, the election is not an end but a beginning.




It’s important that we be ready to advocate for new policies that get us out of the forever gerrymandering wars. Restoring the Voting Rights Act, for a start. Protect Democracy is pushing for 

proportional representation

, both because it provides a pathway to meaningful alternative parties, which we desperately need, and because it also allows states to be more representative of their population. Plus, it can be implemented without a change in the Constitution.




We’ll need these kinds of bootstrapping solutions that move us closer to the democracy we have always deserved. Thankfully a range of groups are trying to help us fill this need: 

Issue One

 has been gathering policymakers to create legislation to steer money out of politics and reduce executive overreach — which 

did not start

 with the Trump administration. 

Go From Here

 is aiming to grow multiracial working class power using new rights, legal rules and governing strategies. 

Democracy Revival Center

 has been offering trainings called “How to Fix Our Broken System.” They offer a set of options on what we can do to get out of the authoritarian doomloop, echoing ideas like proportional representation, expanding the courts and subjecting judges to actual ethical guidelines.




These are important structural fixes that need to be joined with policies that directly speak to the “affordability” crisis. This crisis, just newly discovered by the media, has been around for my entire lifetime — folks struggling to get by on wages that are too low and health care costs that are too high. Pollsters tell us 

“Medicare for All”

 and other ways of saying guaranteed health care for everyone in the U.S. keep growing in popularity. 




This Sustain work isn’t just big national policies. There is a lot that needs to be done in our local communities to reengage civil society and experiment with new versions of community to rebuild trust and repair. I’ve been inspired by many groups, like Michelle Alexander and Nyle Fort’s 

Spirit of Justice

, which is experimenting with new religious formations; or 

Common Justice

, which is modeling alternatives to incarceration in New York City that are victim-centered and result in a stronger community — not the diminished one offered by the carceral state.




All this to say, it took a lot to end this devastating chapter of Trump 2.0. Now let’s exhale, appreciate the unsung folks behind this historic win, and roll up our sleeves — there’s much work to be done in this next chapter.

Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
