title: The fight after the vote
content:
This article 

The fight after the vote

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The good news is that the courts closed off most of the routes by which the Trump administration could have impeded, intimidated or purged voters before Election Day. On September 14, the Supreme Court blocked the Postal Service’s restrictions on mail ballots, and in June it 

upheld

 grace periods for ballots postmarked by Election Day. The Justice Department has reportedly lost nearly all of its 30 lawsuits seeking states’ voter files. And federal law already bars armed federal agents from polling places, a protection seven states reinforced this year by advancing bans of their own.




Pressure doesn’t disappear when one door closes. It moves to the next one. With the front end of the election largely protected, the softer targets are now the count, certification and the seating of the new House.




What to expect




The most likely danger is also the most familiar: a fraud story built on slow counts. Fourteen states and the District of Columbia count ballots that arrive after Election Day, so in many places the results will take days. That delay is normal, and it’s a sign the system is working. But it’s also an opening for anyone who wants to claim that votes counted later are suspect, and the ground is already prepared. One 

survey

 found that fewer than half of voters expect a fair election.




The second danger may already be under way. The “

sanctuary surge

” the administration announced in late September is bringing immigration enforcement into 11 states in the days before the vote. The Homeland Security secretary says agents will appear at polling places only in response to “a threat” or with a warrant. Whatever happens at the polls, the surge’s real effect may be to frighten eligible voters in immigrant and mixed-status families into staying home.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










After the votes are cast, the fight shifts to close races. Democrats need a net gain of about six seats to win the House, so a handful of tight contests could decide who controls it. Expect recounts and lawsuits in every one of them. Expect, too, that some county boards will refuse to certify results. Courts have forced certification every time a board has tried this since 2020, but each refusal buys time and headlines for the story that something went wrong.




Two darker scenarios are less likely but would do far more damage. The first is the seizure of ballots or voting machines by federal authorities. That would break the chain of custody that makes results trustworthy, and it isn’t hypothetical: The FBI has already raided election offices in Fulton County, Georgia, and Maricopa County, Arizona. The second would be a fight over seating the new House on January 3, in which a newly installed House clerk could leave contested Democrats off the roll. Scholars call that far-fetched, and it could only work if control of the House rests on a handful of seats. But the fact that it’s being discussed at all tells us how much of our democracy now depends on officials choosing to follow the rules.




The work after the vote




What can grassroots groups and local officials do once the polls close? The honest answer is that the most useful work will be slow and procedural. It isn’t glamorous. It comes down to three things: making sure every valid ballot is counted, making sure certification happens on time, and keeping the public calm while both are under way.




The first 72 hours matter most. The deadlines to fix rejected ballots, known as cure deadlines, run only a few days, so coalitions should be helping voters amend ballot mistakes right away, while trained observers watch the count. Their public message should be simple and repeated until it sinks in: Slow counts are normal. Local election officials have a parallel job. They can give daily public updates on the count, open counting rooms to observers from all sides, secure ballots and machines, and refuse to release any of them without a court order.




Over the following two weeks, the action moves to county canvass and certification meetings. Coalitions should attend every one, document problems and report them to election protection lawyers, and thank election workers in public, because many of them have been threatened for doing their jobs. Officials, for their part, should certify on time and say in advance that they will, with county and city attorneys ready to go to court the same day any board refuses.




From then through January 3, the work is endurance. Coalitions need to stay organized through recounts and lawsuits, keep local reporters supplied with accurate numbers, and hold mass mobilization in reserve for a real trigger rather than spending it early. Local officials can issue joint statements across party lines affirming the results, and coordinate with their state attorney general on any federal demand for ballots or equipment.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













A few principles hold through the whole period. The first is that losers conceding matters as much as winners winning. A local candidate who loses and says so plainly does more for public trust than any press release, so ask them to do it. The second is to witness, not obstruct. If federal agents try to take ballots or equipment, the grassroots job is to film, call lawyers and alert officials. Physically blocking agents would hand over the pretext for a much wider crackdown. The third is that sheriffs and police chiefs have a particular role to play. They can say publicly that they will protect counting sites and lawful assembly, and that they answer to state law on election materials. The fourth is to use unusual messengers: Republicans, veterans, clergy and business owners vouching for the local count will reach people that advocacy groups never will. And the last is to hold on to the volunteers. Whoever shows up in November should be invited into a standing structure before December, whatever the result.




If the result holds, don’t stand down




That last point matters more than any other, because it’s where the breakthrough trap begins. The breakthrough trap is the pattern in which a movement wins a breakthrough, an election or a transition, and then goes home, while the forces it defeated regroup, wait and come back. It has happened around the world. It happened here. In 2020 we won, exhaled and demobilized. Four years later, the movement we had beaten returned with a plan, a party and a governing agenda we never matched.




A House majority won in November will not spell safety. It will be an opening, and openings close. The people who show up this fall to watch the count and defend the result are the beginning of something we’ve never had enough of: a permanent grassroots demand system that can hold new leaders to account and defend what we win.




Winning is the breakthrough. Holding it is the job.

title: Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?
content:
This article 

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Tomorrow’s midterm elections are widely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second presidency. 

Prior studies

 have found strong associations between protest and U.S. election outcomes, including the 

2010

 and 

2018

 midterm elections. Protests can influence popular 

opinion

 on policy issues, boost turnout among eligible voters, and shape how candidates 

set policy priorities

.




At the Crowd Counting Consortium, or CCC, we have tallied an 

extraordinary number of protests

 since Donald Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025. The majority of protests in Trump’s second term so far have named democracy or the presidency itself as a primary claim — think the nationwide Hands Off and No Kings protests in 2025 and 2026. 




But among protests focused on more specific policy domains, one key theme stands out. The administration’s anti-immigration policies and expansive, violent crackdown on immigrants have generated active, grassroots support 

networks

 in neighborhoods across the country and fueled a wave of protests in support of immigrants’ rights. During Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis and St. Paul, protests took place in over 30 percent of counties containing 80 percent of the nation’s population. March 2026 may have been the month with the highest number of pro-immigrant protests in U.S. history. A significant proportion of these protests occurred in counties that Trump won in 2024. 




Trends in immigration-related protests since January 20, 2017




Of course, the current wave of protest builds on a longer-term foundation of pro-immigrant demonstrations. Since the CCC started collecting data on protest in the United States in 2017, we’ve seen that protests against the federal government’s immigration policies have been a constant feature of the protest landscape across all three presidential administrations — Trump 1, Biden and Trump 2 (see Table 1). 




Table 1: Immigration protest events as a share of all left/liberal protests







Little more than a week after Trump’s first inauguration in January 2017, numerous protests took place around the country in response to his Jan. 27 signing of Executive Order 13769, sometimes called the “Muslim Ban,” which restricted citizens of seven majority-Muslim countries from entering the U.S. On Jan. 28 and 29, mass protests occurred in and around airports, where immigrant rights groups and community members assembled to ensure the safe arrival of citizens of those countries who were in transit when the executive order went into effect. Protests against the executive order continued in February 2017 under the slogan “No Ban No Wall.” The Trump administration ultimately revised the executive order to a narrower version that the U.S. Supreme Court upheld as lawful; multiple protests followed on June 26, 2018. 




But the biggest jumps in protest participation came on coordinated, nationwide days of action related to the administration’s immigration policies. The first, on June 30, 2018, was a national day of action declaring that “Families Belong Together.” These protests demanded an end to the administration’s “child separation policy” — the practice of separating migrant children from parents and caretakers upon arrival at the U.S.-Mexico border — which was in effect under the Obama administration but escalated under Trump. This protest campaign was highly effective: The pressure placed on the administration led the White House to end the policy through an 

executive order

, though loopholes remained.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










On Jan. 19, 2019, the third annual Women’s March on Washington represented an additional increase in coordinated nationwide protests in which immigrants’ rights were a core issue. And July 12, 2019 saw the 

Lights for Liberty

 day of action, which attempted to pressure elected officials (particularly in the newly Democratic Congress) to close detention centers and adopt more humane immigration policies. Ultimately, congressional Democrats introduced legislation in 2021 to reunite immigrant children with their families. In sum, the first Trump administration saw an impressive range of protests on behalf of immigrants’ rights, some of which had powerful impacts. 




Overall, the Biden administration saw a decline in such protests, with about 60 percent fewer than during the first Trump administration (seven percent to 11 percent as a share of overall left/liberal protests, respectively). Notable days of action during the Biden administration included continued protests calling for closure of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention centers, as well as protests against ongoing family detention and separation practices, and protests against asylum restrictions during a major surge in deportations in 2024. 




During the second Trump administration, such protests have seen a breathtaking rise. 




Figure 1 provides a comparative view of the number of immigration-related protests under the second Trump administration, compared to the first. The y-axis, showing the cumulative number of immigration-related protests since Trump’s two inaugurations, demonstrates the massive scale and steady climb of protests during his second term so far.




Figure 1: Counts of pro-immigrant protest events during Trump’s first and second terms







Figure 2 shows the frequency of such events on a monthly basis. There have been more protests in support of immigrants in seven of the months since January 2025 than in any of the 48 months of Trump’s first term. In 10 of the first 17 months of the current term, protests against Trump’s immigration policies made up over 20 percent of total protests. Few other protest claims have animated the public with such enduring salience over time.




Figure 2: Pro-immigrant protests in the U.S., January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Figure 2 also shows clear increases in the number of immigration-related protests during nationwide anti-Trump protests. Spikes in activity occurred on April 19, 2025 during the Hands Off protests; on October 18, 2025, when many No Kings protests adopted opposition to ICE and Trump’s mass deportation agenda as a central claim; and on March 28, 2026, when the third No Kings protests again made immigration a primary claim. Our tallies have also documented 170 repeater events (protests that are scheduled to take place daily, weekly or monthly) that specifically mention immigrant rights or opposition to ICE in their stated claims.




In Illinois and Minnesota, protests started local and went national




Trump’s immigration policies have produced particularly intense local mobilizations in areas that saw escalated ICE deployments, which then diffused to solidarity protests nationwide. For example, from early September to mid-November 2025, ICE launched Operation Midway Blitz targeting immigrants in Chicago. During that period, the CCC documented 3,491 protest events in opposition to Trump’s immigration policies, starting in Chicago and spreading across the country during the No Kings mobilization on Oct. 18, 2025, which named immigration as a central issue.




Operation Metro Surge

, the federal immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis-St. Paul region, also provoked powerful opposition locally and beyond, with over 4,400 protests taking place between Dec. 2, 2025 and Jan. 31, 2026. Significant numbers of protests responded to specific, publicized government abuses, such as aggressive law enforcement actions against immigrants, the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, and the detention of a 5-year-old child of a Colombian immigrant. Three waves of action stood out: the ICE Out For Good weekend of action on Jan. 10-11; the Day of Truth & Freedom on Jan. 23, which was concentrated in Minnesota; and the National Shutdown and ICE Out of Everywhere actions, which mainly spanned Jan. 30-31, with some events lasting into Feb. 1. 




Figure 3 shows the number of counties that saw pro-immigrant protests in Illinois and Minnesota, respectively, after Operation Midway began in Chicago and Operation Metro Surge began in Minneapolis-St. Paul. Overall, these two states saw higher-than-average numbers of counties featuring protests, including among counties far afield from the major cities in which ICE focused its deployments. 




Figure 3. Pro-immigrant protests in Illinois and Minnesota during and after ICE operations in Chicago and Minneapolis-St. Paul







Nationwide, the total volume of protest produced during early 2026 is extraordinary. 




January 2026 alone featured the fourth-most protest events recorded in all 10 years of CCC data, owing to the massive number of protests in Minnesota and around the country in opposition to Operation Metro Surge and its impacts, and to Trump’s immigration agenda in general. 




And the events in Minnesota seem to have been a flashpoint. Anti-ICE protests continued in February and March 2026, and anti-ICE claims were central to the nationwide No Kings mobilization on March 28. March 2026 may have been the month with the highest number of pro-immigrant protests in U.S. history (see Table 2).




Table 2: Top 10 months by total protest events, January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Protests opposing Trump’s immigration policies were reported in 933 counties during Operation Metro Surge, between Dec. 2, 2025 and Feb. 1, 2026 — about 30 percent of all counties in the U.S. These counties were densely populated: Together, they contain more than 80 percent of the U.S. population (see Figure 4). From March 2026 through May 2026, the CCC continued to record thousands of events protesting ICE, with hundreds of distinct civic organizations and hundreds of thousands of people participating. 




Figure 4: U.S. immigration protests following ICE deployments to Minneapolis







Nor are protests against ICE operations an exclusively liberal phenomenon. Instead, there has been a stark increase over time in the number of pro-immigrant protests in counties that Trump won in 2024 by at least a 5-point margin (see Figure 5). Among the pro-immigrant protests that occurred in March 2026, about 40 percent of them occurred in such counties. 




Figure 5: Pro-immigrant protests in counties Trump won by >5 Points in the 2024 Presidential Election, January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Across the country, a broad range of constituencies using a variety of means have expressed opposition to Trump’s immigration policy. Demonstrations have just been one method. Those activating on behalf of and in support of immigrants include people forming human chains to 

protect

 immigrant workers; neighborhoods organizing support networks for affected immigrant families; students engaging in 

walkouts

 from schools and protests at college 

career fairs

; people engaging in 

hunger strikes

 in support of international and undocumented students; 

knitters

 engaging in “craftivism”; people holding 

encampments

 outside of ICE facilities or 

noise demonstrations

 outside of hotels in which ICE agents were housed; consumers engaging in boycotts and sell-backs at 

Target 

and 

Home Depot

; clergy engaging in 

civil disobedience

; communities holding 

vigils 

for slain immigrants or those killed while advocating for them; community members building 

raised beds

 across thoroughfares to prevent ICE vehicles from accessing facilities, and more. Institutions and employers have raised their voices: Local businesses and business associations have called for the end of ICE operations in their towns, ranchers and farmers have decried treatment of their immigrant employees, and the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops has condemned mistreatment of immigrants as well.




Counter-protest was minimal




Trump’s immigration policies 

have supporters

 in the country, particularly among Republicans. But few people have rallied or marched in defense of them. Right-leaning protests made up fewer than two percent of all immigration-related protests during the first 14 months of the first Trump administration, and less than 0.7 percent of immigration-related protests during the same stretch of his second administration. 




The frequency of pro-immigrant protests during Trump’s second term has eclipsed that of anti-immigration protests by 145 to 1. The vast majority of anti-immigration protests have been counter-protests occurring at demonstrations in support of immigrants and their rights. 




However, right-leaning protests have been increasingly characterized by anti-immigrant claims over the past three presidencies. Whereas anti-immigrant protests constituted 1.68 percent of all right-learning protests during Trump’s first term, that proportion has increased sevenfold so far during his second, to 12.43 percent. 




Table 3: Anti-immigration protest events as a share of all right/conservative protests







A powerful and growing pro-immigrant constituency




Today’s mass protests in support of immigrants’ rights build on a durable pattern of pro-immigrant and anti-ICE protest in the U.S. To wit, the CCC has documented a prayer 

protest

 outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois that has been held every Friday for the past 20 years. 




But the recent increase in pro-immigrant protests and their intensity is notable. The breadth and volume of pro-immigrant protests show that committed activists and organizations have succeeded in rallying huge numbers in favor of justice and dignity for immigrants, indicating a durable underlying infrastructure. In this essay, we focused on street protest as one indicator in the overall picture. But community mobilization on behalf of immigrants has meant far more than demonstrations. Mutual aid and neighborly support, observing and documenting ICE operations, litigation, support to immigrants in detention, and direct appeals to public officials have all been central to America’s response to Trump’s immigration policies. The growth of pro-immigrant protests reflects a (potentially growing) constituency willing to take risks to defend a multicultural vision of America, potentially widening its appeal. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













In short, we see capable organizers and the mass public pushing hard for humane treatment of immigrants for the foreseeable future. Neither political party has figured out how to address immigration in a way that resolves the need for safe and secure borders and the need to treat everyone on U.S. soil with dignity, decency and due process. But the impacts of Trump’s policies on immigrants, their families and their broader communities provide a galvanizing issue for Americans who otherwise agree on little else. For example, some 

conservative faith communities

 and various progressive groups increasingly find themselves on the same side when it comes to immigration. 




Policymakers often resist turning to activists, civil society organizations and community groups for policy solutions. But the persistence of multi-sectoral immigration activism, as seen through protest alone, also reflects a powerful and growing constituency in favor of just and humane approaches to immigration. Protests reflect and shape the existing moral consensus but also can reorient constituencies in favor of a new consensus. We hope the members of the next Congress pay attention.

author: Neesha Powell
title: A North Carolina movement asks voters to reject corporate tax breaks
content:
This article 

A North Carolina movement asks voters to reject corporate tax breaks

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The affordability crisis is hitting people hard across the country, but it’s especially acute in North Carolina. For 

the sixth year

 in a row, North Carolina holds the distinction of being the worst state in the nation for workers based on its wage policies, worker protections, and rights to organize, according to Oxfam. 

Nearly half of renters

 in the state are struggling to afford their homes, while nearly a third of households are cost-burdened (spending over 30 percent of their income on housing).




North Carolina voters’ eyes may light up when they see 

two proposed constitutional amendments

 on their November ballots: one to cap the state personal and corporate income tax rates at 3.5 percent, down from a cap of seven percent, and another to limit how much local governments can levy in property taxes. On their face, they appear as if they might bring much-needed tax relief to North Carolina’s working class. 




The amendments are deceptively framed as being beneficial to working people and homeowners, reading as if they would lower individual taxes when there’s no indication that they will, according to Todd Warren, statewide campaign strategist at Down Home North Carolina, a member-led organization that endorsed a “no” vote. Instead, Warren said, the measures would be a giveaway to corporations and wealthy individuals by limiting how much they pay toward the public good — and a “scam” for voters.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Since the passage of the two Republican-sponsored bills that placed the amendments on the ballot this past May, Down Home NC and over 20 other groups have come together as the 

NC Vote Against coalition

 to defeat them, as well as to oppose a third amendment that would enshrine voter identification requirements in the state constitution.




Each organization has its own expertise and its own tactics, but a common message: The amendments will not benefit working-class people, but rather corporations and the ultra-wealthy. Each group is playing its part in collecting a total of 100,000 pledges from North Carolinians who commit to voting against the amendments.




The fight to fund the future




Down Home NC joined together with another coalition member, the Carolina Federation, to launch the 

Fund the Future campaign

, deploying nearly 200 paid canvassers.  




Jenn Frye, co–director of the Carolina Federation, spent part of this weekend canvassing at the poll at a Durham, North Carolina library, where she convinced an older couple to vote “no” on the amendments. After a member-led endorsement process that included political education on the amendments, a leadership summit and a vote at a statewide membership meeting, the Carolina Federation decided they wanted to deeply engage in the amendment fight. “We see more and more people in North Carolina who agree that corporations and the wealthiest individuals aren’t contributing what they owe when day in and day out, North Carolinians are working really hard,” Frye said. “We pay our taxes, and we contribute what we owe.”




Down Home NC and the Carolina Federation were founded in 2017 and 2018, respectively, in the wake of President Trump first taking office and Republicans winning control of both North Carolina’s state legislature and governorship in 2013 (for 

the first time

 since Reconstruction). The groups share a long-term goal of loosening corporate power’s grip on the state legislature and supplanting it with people power.




The 

Fund the Future campaign

 campaign is knocking doors, talking to voters at the polls, getting resolutions against the amendments passed by local governments and school boards, and placing signs in small businesses and in yards, among other tactics. So far, the Carolina Federation’s canvassers have knocked on over 600,000 doors across six counties, collecting over 33,000 pledges, while Down Home NC’s canvassers had knocked 500,000 doors across 20 counties and collected about 8,000 pledges.




“Whatever the outcome of this amendment fight, Federation’s members plan to launch a statewide campaign next year with other organizations like Down Home and 

Siembra

 to demand that the legislature pass fair tax policies that make corporations and the wealthiest individuals pay what they owe our communities in taxes,” Frye said. “That may be a multi-year fight. It is one our members feel is worth waging.”




North Carolinians deserve funding for real solutions, Frye said, such as property tax assistance programs, childcare tax credits, an increased minimum wage (it’s currently the federal minimum, $7.25 per hour), and protections against corporate landlords.




Todd Warren of Down Home NC said he has never seen such a robust response to a single issue in over 20 years of working and organizing in North Carolina.




Because Down Home NC’s chapters run organizing campaigns to make sure that local budgets go toward working people’s needs, members recognized immediately how the amendments would exacerbate the underfunding of local services. Like the Carolina Federation, its members endorsed a “no” vote in addition to endorsing political candidates who are supportive of its platforms.




Many voters don’t know about the amendments, Frye said, and if they do, they’re often not sure what to make of them or inclined to support them because they’re exhausted and stressed out due to the affordability crisis. But when they are engaged in conversation about how the amendments affect services they rely on, “then people are movable,” she said.




North Carolina residents march to the polls with signs opposing tax amendments on the ballot during early voting in Guilford County on Oct. 27, 2026. (Guilford For All)




Frye gave the example of her own mother, who recently suffered a series of strokes. Fortunately she was living in a North Carolina county with adequately funded Emergency Medical Services, or EMS. But residents of counties with underfunded EMS operations could face a life-or-death situation during medical emergencies.




“Right now, people feel like ‘taxes’ is a dirty word,” said Warren, a former public school teacher. “But if they connect it to something that they care about, like, ‘Oh, in Johnston County, we have explosive population growth. We need to build a new high school. These amendments would limit our ability to [do that].’ Then they’re like, ‘I’m gonna vote “no” on it.’ We can do that in a five-minute organizing conversation. It doesn’t take much for people to see through the scam.” 




North Carolina’s allegiance to corporations




North Carolina has lost out 

on almost $18 billion

 in annual tax revenue since Republicans began overhauling the tax system in 2013. Personal income tax reforms are so regressive that the state’s lowest earners pay 

more than 10

 percent of their income in state and local taxes, while the highest earners pay only six percent. For corporations, the income tax has dropped from seven percent to two percent, the 

lowest in the nation

, and will be phased out completely by 2030. As tax revenue shrinks, so does local governments’ ability to fully fund vital public services.




“Our public services, the things that are supposed to strengthen our communities and support all families in all counties in North Carolina, are being stretched to the limit by the tax cuts,” Frye said. “These amendments want to take that and enshrine it into the [state] constitution.”




Exploitation has marked North Carolina’s economy since the days of chattel slavery. Post-slavery, Black families like my own (in Bertie County) sharecropped for a living well into the 20th century — jobs now carried out by migrant workers who 

experience poor labor conditions

. The Duke family once had a monopoly on the state’s tobacco industry and founded both 

Duke Energy

 and 

Duke University

, two institutions notorious for not paying their fair share.




Now the state and some local governments are subsidizing data centers, of which 

over 60

 have been built and at least 30 more are planned or under construction. Under pressure, the state eliminated some tax breaks for data centers in July, but three remaining sales tax subsidies are projected to rob the state of $250 million in revenue annually. Meanwhile, between 2017 to 2024, the average electricity bill of a North Carolina household 

rose by nearly 30

 percent. The state is subsidizing wealthy corporations as regular folks struggle to keep their lights on.




A history of underfunded public schools




On May Day this year, thousands gathered in the capital city, Raleigh, to rally for fully funded schools. Tax cuts have already contributed to the state being ranked last in the country 

in public school funding

 by GDP.




Isabell Moore, a coordinator at North Carolina Families for Public Schools (a project of Down Home NC) and a public school parent, said the amendments could be “catastrophic” for public education. North Carolina Families for Public Schools comprises countywide, districtwide and schoolwide teams of volunteer organizers who are calling for equitable, fully funded public schools. These teams are currently 

circulating a pledge

 to fund the future for children that includes voting against the amendments, along with measures like fair funding for special education; higher teacher pay; and safe, inclusive schools for all students, including those from immigrant families. 




North Carolina Families for Public Schools had already voted on its 2026 platform when the amendments dropped in May but decided to incorporate them because they stand directly in the way of their goal to win fully funded schools. Their organizers have been tapping into their personal networks to turn people out to vote against the amendments, holding house parties and school-based parties to educate people on the amendments, and more. 




“Everyday working people and public school parents are creative and tough and scrappy,” Moore said. “If we commit to not just voting ‘no’ but also organizing other people in our networks and in our school communities, that’s when we really start to build the power to defeat the amendments.”
















Support Us

Donate













Even public schools in wealthy counties like Durham, home to Duke University (which has a 

$14.3 billion endowment

) and Duke University Health System (which made 

nearly $766 million

 in profits last year), 

are chronically underfunded

. The riches of these two tax-exempt nonprofit institutions haven’t trickled down. Among other demands, the Durham Rising coalition—made up of workers, students, and community members—is calling for Duke University to help fund public schools and educator salaries by making a voluntary payment to the local government 

called a PILOT

, or payment in lieu of taxes.




Since the summer, Christy Patterson, vice president of the Durham chapter of the North Carolina Association of Educators, or NCAE, and a middle school teacher for students with disabilities, has been knocking on doors to tell folks the amendments are for billionaires, not everyday people. The NCAE, which functions as a professional organization because North Carolina bans public-sector collective bargaining, is part of the NC Vote Against coalition and was one of the main architects of the “Kids Over Corporations” rally in May.




“Our voters and our community are engaging us in conversation on the doors,” Patterson said. “We’ve had some conversations that really made us think. Constructive friction on the doors is always good because everybody’s not going to say the same thing or think the same. They’re just so ready to open the door and talk to us, so we are grateful for that.”




Organizing for the long run




In a September poll

 by Elon University, 67 percent of respondents were in favor of the income tax amendment, and 72 percent supported the property tax amendment. Organizers are working hard to turn that tide.




However, even if they don’t get their desired outcome, there is an entire movement that will continue holding North Carolina corporations and wealthy households accountable until they contribute their fair share to the public good. Organizations like the Carolina Federation, Down Home NC, and the NCAE have been engaging in this work for years and are in it for the long haul.




Warren hopes the Fund the Future campaign can help shift the narrative so that people understand that “taxes” aren’t inherently bad but rather a tool for improving quality of life for themselves, their families, and their communities. 




“Through years of listening and campaigning, we know what working people across North Carolina want,” Warren said: well-funded, well-staffed public schools, healthcare access, transportation options and recreation programs for kids, infrastructure for effective disaster response. “When we talk to people about those things, even when they understand that it may involve an increase in taxes for them personally, they support funding those types of programs.”

How Serbian students toppled a dictator

On Oct. 25, Serbia voted and the Student List won. Late that evening, President Aleksandar Vučić — the man who has dominated the country’s politics since 2012, steadily hollowing out its courts, media and elections along the way — went on television and admitted that his Serbian Progressive Party and its allies had lost. The final count isn’t in yet, but the result is not in doubt. Candidates selected by the Students List protest movement have more than half the vote and a majority in the 250-seat parliament.




For more than 20 years, our team at the Belgrade-based Center for Applied NonViolent Actions and Strategies, or CANVAS, has worked with activists from dozens of countries on one question: How do ordinary people defeat a government that looks unbeatable? This time the answer came from our own streets, again. We want to explain what happened, because movements elsewhere will try to learn from it, and we’d like them to learn the right lessons.

title: Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy
content:

Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy

I recently showed up to a protest for the first time in months, looked around, and thought: “Who the hell 

are

 all these people?” 




Friends I could once rely on running into at protests when I was younger were missing. 




The fact that I hadn’t been to a protest in months was unusual. I’d had a hard season of exhaustion and cynicism, and I felt I was falling out of the loop. In the last few years, I turned 30 and moved back to my hometown, and the once-intense focus on social movements that I had in my 20s was now jostling for attention with work and family. 




The absence of my comrades at that protest seemed to signal that others, too, had burned or faded out of organizing.




It’s a trend that Chris Dixon describes in his new book, which is about sticking around for the long haul in the fight for a better world: “In radical activist scenes especially,” he writes, “people tend to age out by their 30s, if not before.” 




When the manuscript of Dixon’s book came my way, it spoke to my fear of burning or fading out of the movements that have given my life meaning and momentum. After Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration moved to rein in the Bovino-style spectacle with its made-for-TV arrests. In an attempt to avoid another public outcry, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly settled into a new rhythm.




Arrests have still increased month after month, reaching 

a record high

The

 

New York Times

 

reported

, this phase is “captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.”
